summary: Defines terminology, a problem statement, and requirements for running IKE and IPsec on clusters of machines. It also describes gaps in standards and implementations that need filling so clusters from different vendors can interoperate with peers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: What if one secure connection is handled by a team of computers acting as one? This explains the problems and what is needed so teams from different makers work with others.

questions: ike on a cluster of gateways
subtitle: Why clustering IPsec gateways is hard, and what needs fixing.

tldr.problem: IPsec and IKE maintain large amounts of state (encryption keys, counters, policies) that changes frequently. Running them on a cluster of gateways requires synchronizing this state, which is impractical at scale.
tldr.mechanism: This document identifies specific challenges: IKE message counters, IPsec packet counters, synchronization gaps, and issues with different cluster architectures (hot standby vs. load sharing). It outlines the trade-offs for each problem.
tldr.outcome: Vendors and operators understand the gaps in standards and implementations, allowing future protocol extensions to enable interoperable IPsec clusters from different vendors.

facts.label: Typical gateway capacity
facts.value: Thousands to hundreds of thousands of SAs

today: RFC 6027 is an Informational RFC that identifies gaps in clustering IPsec. It has not been obsoleted and serves as the problem statement for future standardization efforts in clustering IKE and IPsec gateways.

sections.title: The Clustering Demand
sections.content:
As VPN deployments become more critical to organizations, there is demand for IPsec cluster solutions that provide both high availability (through redundancy) and scalability (through load sharing). IKE and IPsec, however, store more state and change it more frequently than protocols like DHCP or DNS, making them harder to cluster.

In general, deploying IKE and IPsec in a cluster requires synchronizing so much information among cluster members that it becomes impractical. Alternatively, if less information is synchronized, failover becomes slow and defeats the purpose of having a cluster.

This document defines terminology and describes the specific problems that arise. It targets members of the IETF community developing solutions for IPsec clusters that can interoperate across vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: One bank teller knows all the customers and their secrets. If three tellers act as one, they must all know the same secrets and remember which customers already came in, or trouble follows.

sections.title: Types of Clusters
sections.content:
A cluster is a set of two or more IPsec gateways implementing the same security policy and protecting the same domain. They exist to provide high availability and scalability.

Hot standby clusters (HS) have only one active member at a time; others are standbys. The Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) is one way to build these.

Load sharing clusters (LS) have multiple active members simultaneously, distributing traffic among them. Load sharing is more efficient but more complex.

Clusters can be tight (all members share one IP address via VRRP or multicast) or loose (each member has a different IP address). In a tight cluster, peers need only know one address. In a loose cluster, peers use DNS or IKEv2 redirect mechanisms to find the right member.

A synch channel is the internal communication path among cluster members for sharing state. This channel may be IP-based or proprietary, but its use must be minimized for scalability.
sections.plainLanguage: Backup tellers (standby) wait to take over if the active one fails. Or multiple tellers work at once (load sharing). They might share a phone number (tight) or each have their own (loose).

sections.title: State Synchronization Challenges
sections.content:
IKE and IPsec maintain long-lived state: IKE Security Associations last minutes to days and carry keys and information; IPsec SAs last minutes to hours. Some gateways carry hundreds of thousands of these.

IKE message counters are critical: each peer must process IKE messages in order, skipping no message IDs. When a member fails over, it must know the last message IDs both sent and received, or the peer will reject its messages and the entire IKE SA will be dropped.

IPsec packet counters (anti-replay) prevent duplicate packets. After failover, the newly active member must not reuse a counter number that has been used, or the peer drops the packet as a duplicate attack.

Inbound counter synchronization is even tougher: if a packet arrives at a newly active member, there is no way to know if it is a replay without seeing the entire history. One solution is to disable anti-replay verification after failover (allowed by standards but a policy decision), or to rekey all child SAs after failover.

Missing synch messages can doom an IKE SA: if the active member creates a new child SA using message N, the synch message might be lost before failover. The newly active member will not have the SA and its IKE message counter will be out of sync, causing peer rejection.
sections.plainLanguage: Each conversation with a customer must follow a script: message 1, message 2, message 3. If a teller falls and another takes over at message 4 but doesn't know the script reached message 3, the customer hangs up. Passwords also age: if a teller gives out password number 500 and falls, the new teller cannot use numbers 1-500 again.

sections.title: Load Sharing and Sticky Sessions
sections.content:
In load sharing clusters, all active members may need to use the same SAs. This creates new problems.

The sticky approach routes all traffic with a peer (or matching a specific policy entry) through the same cluster member. This avoids counter synchronization because the same member handles all packets for an SA. But sticky routing leads to uneven load distribution, especially when one SA carries significant traffic.

The duplicate approach creates multiple parallel SAs with the same selectors for each active member. Different packets go through different members with different SAs. The downside: peers see redundant SAs that they do not need, and different packets in the same flow may be protected by different SAs, which might confuse firewalls or stateful inspectors.

Counter modes (like CTR and GCM ciphers) require that the initial vector is never repeated. For shared SAs across members, cluster members must coordinate to avoid generating the same initial vector, adding another synchronization problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Either route all calls from a customer to one teller (sticky, uneven), or let any teller take the call with a copy of the secret (duplicate, but confusing to the customer). Some secrets use a timer: if two tellers start at the same time, they must coordinate so the timer counts differently.

sections.title: IP Addresses and SPI Allocation
sections.content:
Different IP addresses for IKE and IPsec: Many implementations use a cluster IP address for tunnel-mode IPsec traffic but individual member IP addresses for IKE packets. To the peer, this looks odd (usually both come from the same address) and may be dropped by unmodified peers. Solutions include NAT or assigning multiple addresses to interfaces, but neither is feasible for all implementations.

SPI allocation (Security Parameter Index): each SA must have a unique SPI relative to the peer. In a cluster, each member must generate SPIs that avoid collisions with other members. The means of achieving this is a local matter, outside the scope of standards.
sections.plainLanguage: If IKE comes from teller A's phone and IPsec packets come from the team phone, the customer thinks something is wrong. Each teller's secret handshake code (SPI) must be unique or confusion follows.
